titolo: Could America Survive Another Great Depression? Here's the Truth

numero.sotto: HOW MUCH THE DOW LOST BY 1932

descrizione:
The stock market lost almost nine tenths of its value. Thousands of banks failed. One worker in four lost a job. So could it happen again? We break down the four things that turned a crash into a catastrophe in 1929, and check which ones have been fixed.

From bank runs and a shrinking money supply to the gold standard, plus the Japanese finance minister who escaped the Depression early, we follow the story on animated maps. And we look at the one safety net that is getting thinner every year: the national debt.
tag: could america survive another great depression

scene.testo: A bank run in a single day. A gold promise that drowned a nation. And a debt cushion getting thinner. Could America survive again?
In October 1929, the American stock market began to fall, and it kept falling for almost three years.
By the summer of 1932, the Dow had lost 89 percent of its value. More than 9,000 banks had failed.
The economy shrank by nearly a third, and about one in four workers had no job.
It would take the market 25 years to get back to where it started.
Now jump to 2020. Unemployment leaped to 14.7 percent in a single month, the highest on record. Yet the economy bounced back.
So could America survive another Great Depression? It comes down to four things that broke in 1929.
Three of them have been fixed. One is in worse shape than at any time since World War Two.
And one country found the way out long before America did. But first, the thing that can still break in a single day.
In 1930, a rumor was enough to empty a bank. Deposits had no federal insurance whatsoever.
If you heard your bank was in trouble, you ran to get your money out before everyone else did.
When one bank closed its doors, the line formed at the next one.
In December 1930, the Bank of United States in New York collapsed. It served hundreds of thousands of ordinary families.
Its name made many believe the government stood behind it. It didn't.
With about 200 million dollars in deposits, it was the biggest bank failure in American history up to then.
It was one of more than 9,000 banks that failed by 1933. Depositors lost over 1.3 billion dollars.
Families who had done nothing wrong lost their savings overnight.
By March 1933, the new president closed every bank in the country for a week to stop the panic.

eventi.descrizione: 1930s American president, round glasses, smiling, suit

scene.testo: Then he went on the radio and said your money was safer in a reopened bank than under the mattress.
When the banks reopened, people lined up again. This time, to put their money back in.
That's the first thing that broke: trust in the banks. But a failed bank took something even bigger with it.
When a bank fails, its deposits vanish, and so does all the money it would have lent.
Between 1929 and 1933, the amount of money in America fell by more than a third.
Fewer dollars meant falling prices. Falling prices sound good, until your loan stays the same size.
Picture a farmer selling wheat for less every year, while the bank still wants the same payment.
Businesses cut wages, then jobs. People without jobs spent less, so more businesses cut. The spiral kept going.
The Federal Reserve had the power to stop the money from shrinking. Mostly, it didn't use it.
In 1963, economists Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz showed exactly how much damage that inaction did.

eventi.descrizione: 20th-century American economist, woman, glasses, short hair

scene.testo: Almost 40 years later, a future Fed chairman, Ben Bernanke, told them: you're right, we did it, and we're sorry.

eventi.descrizione: American economist, gray beard, glasses, suit

scene.testo: Thanks to you, he added, we won't do it again. That's the second thing that broke: the money itself.
And part of the reason the Fed held back was the third thing: a promise made of gold.
In 1929, every dollar could be swapped for a fixed amount of gold. To keep that promise, a country couldn't just print money.
When gold started leaving, a country had to raise interest rates, even in the middle of a collapse.
In September 1931, Britain let go of gold. Investors feared America was next and began pulling gold out.
So in October 1931, with banks failing everywhere, the Fed raised interest rates to defend the dollar.
It was like being handcuffed while you're drowning. Meanwhile, Japan made the same bet at the worst moment.
In January 1930, three months after the crash, Japan tied the yen back to gold at its old value.
Prices collapsed and the Japanese countryside was devastated. Then, in December 1931, a new finance minister took over.
His name was Takahashi Korekiyo, and he was 77 years old. On his very first day, he took Japan off gold.

eventi.descrizione: elderly Japanese finance minister, white mustache, 1930s suit

scene.testo: Then he did something almost nobody dared in a depression. He spent. And to pay for it, he borrowed.
From November 1932, the Bank of Japan bought the new government bonds directly. The yen fell, and Japanese goods got cheaper abroad.
Japan became one of the first major economies to climb out of the depression. America held on until April 1933.
That was a year and a half after Britain. Economists later found the pattern: the first to leave gold were the first to recover.
Takahashi's own story ended badly. When he tried to rein in military spending, army officers killed him in February 1936.
He was 81. So that's three things that broke: the banks, the money, and the gold. Have we fixed them?
The banks first. In 1933, Congress created federal deposit insurance. In 1934, only nine banks failed.
In the four years before, more than 9,000 had failed. Nine, against thousands. That's what insurance did.
Today, deposits are insured up to 250,000 dollars per person, per bank. Can a rumor still sink a bank?
Yes. In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank customers tried to pull out 42 billion dollars in a single day, mostly from their phones.
It was the biggest bank run in history. The bank failed the next morning.
But two days later, the government promised every depositor would get their money back. A rumor can sink a bank, not the savers.
Next, the gold. In 1971, the United States cut the dollar's last link to gold.
Today, when the system freezes, the Fed can create the money to unfreeze it. In 2008, it did exactly that.
In September 2008, Lehman Brothers, a giant Wall Street bank, went bankrupt, and the whole financial system seized up.
This time, nobody watched. Within weeks, Congress gave the Treasury up to 700 billion dollars, and the Fed flooded the system with money.
The economy shrank by 4.3 percent and unemployment peaked at 10 percent. Painful, but nothing like losing a third of everything.
In 2020, the pandemic shut the country down. Congress passed a 2.2 trillion dollar relief package, the largest in history.
Unemployment hit 14.7 percent in a single month, then started falling the very next month. That's a safety net working.
And then there's the fourth thing, the one nobody fixed. Look at how both crises were stopped: the government borrowed and spent.
That only works if there's room to borrow. In 1929, federal debt was less than a fifth of the American economy.
Today, debt held by the public is on track to reach 101 percent of the entire economy by the end of 2026.
That's the highest since just after World War Two. The all-time record is 106 percent, set in 1946.
It's projected to pass that record and reach around 120 percent by 2036. This year alone, the government borrows about 1.9 trillion dollars more than it collects.
And debt costs money. This year, America will spend about a trillion dollars just on interest, more than on its entire military.
By 2036, interest is projected to cost almost twice as much as defense. Picture your phone bill doubling while your pay stays flat.
A big debt doesn't cause a depression by itself. But it's the cushion that saved America twice, and every year it gets thinner.
So let's score it. Banks fixed, since insured savings are protected. Money fixed, since the Fed has shown it will step in.
Gold is gone, since the dollar isn't tied to it anymore. And debt is worse than at any time since World War Two.
Could America survive another Great Depression? Probably, yes. Three of the four things that turned a crash into a catastrophe are fixed.
But the fourth one is the safety net itself. In 1929, it took the market 25 years to come back.

eventi.testo: The net is the weak point

scene.testo: The real question isn't whether America would survive the next one. It's how much of the cushion would be left when it comes.
